scenes.headline: What is a Shuffle?
scenes.subtitle: The most expensive operation in Spark — and the number-one lever for performance.
scenes.narration: A shuffle is the most expensive thing Spark does. Understanding it is the single biggest lever you have on performance.

scenes.headline: First, recall how Spark stores data
items: Your dataset is split into many partitions
Each executor processes its own partitions in parallel
No coordination is needed — until keys must meet
scenes.narration: Recall that Spark splits your data into partitions spread across executors, each processed in parallel, with no coordination needed — until keys must come together.

scenes.headline: The problem
scenes.text: Operations like groupBy and join need every row with the same key on the same machine.
scenes.narration: But operations like group-by and join need every row with the same key to live on the same machine.

scenes.headline: So Spark shuffles — in three phases
scenes.narration: To make that happen, Spark shuffles. It writes data bucketed by key, exchanges it across the network, and reducers read back the grouped data.

scenes.headline: One line can trigger it
scenes.code:
# groupBy is a WIDE transformation -> full shuffle
(df.groupBy("region")
   .agg(F.sum("amount"))
   .show())
scenes.narration: This looks innocent, but group-by is a wide transformation. It forces a full shuffle across the entire cluster.

scenes.headline: Why it's so expensive
items: Data is serialized and written to disk as shuffle files
Then sent across the network between executors
Reducers read it back, sort and merge
It's a stage barrier — the next stage waits for all of it
scenes.narration: It's costly because data is serialized to disk, sent over the network, then read, sorted and merged — and it creates a stage barrier where the next stage waits for everything.

scenes.headline: Narrow vs wide transformations
scenes.narration: Narrow transformations like map and filter stay within a partition and are cheap. Wide ones like group-by and join cross partitions and trigger the shuffle.

scenes.headline: How to minimize the shuffle
items: Pre-aggregate before the shuffle (reduceByKey, not groupByKey)
Broadcast the small side of a join
Let AQE coalesce partitions and fix skew
scenes.narration: To tame it: pre-aggregate before shuffling, broadcast small joins, enable adaptive query execution, and right-size your shuffle partitions.

scenes.headline: Turn on the safety nets
scenes.narration: Adaptive Query Execution re-optimizes shuffles at runtime, and a broadcast threshold lets Spark skip the shuffle entirely when one side of a join is small.

scenes.headline: Remember
scenes.text: Every wide transformation triggers a shuffle. You can't always avoid it — but you can design to minimize and tune it.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: every wide transformation triggers a shuffle. You can't always avoid it, but you can design to minimize and tune it.
